1.pericope_label: My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger: deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter

schools.summary: Henry praises the book for teaching not only divine wisdom for another world but human prudence for this, grades the danger so that being bound for a known friend is hazardous and striking hands with a stranger much more so, and allows that the stranger may instead be the creditor, the usurer to whom a man becomes bound although he owes him nothing.

Gill takes the sleeplessness of the fourth verse as a measure of what is at stake, since a man in such circumstances should leave no stone unturned nor method untried to extricate himself, and reads the bare phrase of the fifth verse in the sense of immediately or out of hand, which he says it sometimes bears with the Jewish writers.

Clarke describes what suretyship does to the debtor, whose spirit of exertion is crippled once he knows another stands between him and the demands of law, and who may treat his friend with neglect lest the pledge be reclaimed, and advises pressing him for payment without rest; Wesley explains that the creditor is called a stranger because the usurers of that nation were heathens or reputed as bad, and enters the qualification that suretyship in some cases may be not only lawful but an act of justice and charity.

Ellicott sets the practice in economic history, from a law given before the people took up commerce, when lending on interest to a poor Israelite was forbidden, to the developed trade of Solomon’s time with its distant communications and caravans, when lending on interest and suretyship with it became frequent; he also renders the counsel of the third verse literally, to let oneself be trampled on and to importune. Keil and Delitzsch ask whether the preposition introduces the man for whom or the man with whom one becomes surety, refuse to render the phrase of the fifth verse as immediately since that sense is rabbinic and not biblical, reject a proposed parallelism because a bird-catcher is not at the same time a hunter of gazelles, and derive the two creatures’ names from elegance and from whistling.

debates: Does the fifth verse say immediately? Gill takes the bare phrase in that sense, noting that it sometimes means out of hand with the Jewish writers. Keil and Delitzsch refuse it outright, since the sense is rabbinical and not biblical; they report that the versions render as though the word were out of the snare, that one scholar prefers that reading and another supposes a word for hunter to have fallen out, and object that the proposed parallelism will not stand because a bird-catcher is not at the same time a hunter of gazelles. Ellicott simply supplies a phrase such as the hand that held him.
outliers: Ellicott accounts for the rise of suretyship by the growth of trade, from a time when loans met bare necessity to one of communications with distant countries and caravans beyond the great river.

Clarke describes the moral effect of the transaction on the debtor, whose spirit of exertion is crippled once another carries his burden, and who may avoid his benefactor lest the pledge be reclaimed.
Keil and Delitzsch answer a proposed emendation with a practical objection, that a bird-catcher is not at the same time a hunter of gazelles.
Wesley enters the one qualification the chapter lacks, that suretyship in some cases may be not only lawful but an act of justice and charity.
themes: a law made before commerce
a burden that cripples the man it lifts
trampled on, and importuning
immediately, or out of the snare
a gazelle named from its elegance

6.pericope_label: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: yet a little sleep, a little slumber: so shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth

schools.summary: Henry observes that sluggards must be schooled and that the teacher has found a school low enough for a pupil who will not come to him, since dreaming scholars never love wakeful teachers, and that man, taught more than the beasts of the earth, is so degenerated that he may learn wisdom from the meanest insects and be shamed by them.

Gill answers the ant with authorities, one philosopher for its having no ruler and the naturalists for its working even by moonlight, has it toiling in the heat night and day while the season lasts, traces the gradation of the sluggard’s reply from sound sleeps to slumbers to the folding of the hands, and allows the poverty of the eleventh verse to come either swiftly and unawares or by slow steps but surely.

Clarke answers the verse with natural history and corrects what it seems to say, since the ant sleeps through the winter and does not eat, so that a hoard laid up against it would be useless, and it gathers instead when food is most plentiful; he describes its carrying its young out for the sun and covering the nest against rain with a thin stone, takes the traveller of the eleventh verse as coming with slow but sure steps while the want comes with irresistible fury, and reports a further clause added by three versions and an old English one; Wesley settles the same verse in four words.

Keil and Delitzsch cite the book that makes the beasts our teachers, derive the creature’s names in two languages from industry and from its low unperceived motion, take the three officers of the seventh verse for the highest judiciary, police and executive powers and report two versions that confused the first with the word for harvest, distinguish the late summer heat from the end of harvest in the eighth, and insist that the tenth verse is the sluggard’s own reply to an unwelcome disturber rather than an ironical permission; Ellicott glosses the first officer as properly a judge and notes that the word for the traveller is intensive, one who moves swiftly.

debates: Does the ant lay up in summer against the winter? The proverb is read so by most of them, and Gill has her toiling in the heat because nothing can be got afterwards. Clarke denies the natural fact while keeping the moral: the ant sleeps through the winter and does not eat, so that such a hoard would be useless to it, and what it collects it collects when food is most plentiful, for consumption in the proper season. Keil and Delitzsch avoid the question by distinguishing the two seasons named, the height of the summer heat and the end of harvest.
outliers: Clarke reports his own observation of the ant carrying its young out to lie in the sun and bringing them in before rain, covering the entrance of the nest with a thin stone or tile.
Henry calls the passage a schooling and notes that the teacher had to find a school low enough for a pupil who would not come to him, since dreaming scholars never love wakeful teachers.
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the tenth verse is spoken by the sluggard himself, turning away his disturber, and that its diminutives sound like self-delusion.
Clarke reports a clause added by three versions and an old English one, that if thou wilt be diligent thy harvest shall be as a fountain and poverty shall flee far from thee.
themes: a school low enough for the pupil
an ant that does not eat in winter
three officers the insect does without
the sluggard answering back
poverty at a walk or at a run

12.pericope_label: A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth: he winketh with his eyes: these six things doth the Lord hate; yea, seven are an abomination unto him

schools.summary: Henry would have had the phrase of the twelfth verse left untranslated, since the term is often used in Scripture, and takes the man for one who makes a trade of doing evil, especially with his tongue, carrying his designs with the subtlety of the serpent.

Gill divides the two words of the twelfth verse into the unprofitable man and the lawless one, notes that Belial is a name of the devil and applies the character to the man of sin, keeps the wink to the air and gesture of a sneering man signalling to a friend at another’s weakness, and observes that pride heads the list because it was probably the first sin committed, of the angels and of the first man.

Clarke refers the name to the first man when he lost his innocence, holds that the signs of the thirteenth verse are spoken of debauchees and quotes a Latin elegy on the signals lovers make at a banquet, saying the rest of it cannot be introduced here, guesses that the breaking of the fifteenth verse alludes to stoning, and glosses each of the seven hated things, ending with the man who troubles the peace of a family, a village or a state; Wesley makes the swift feet those who greedily execute their wicked designs.

Keil and Delitzsch ask which part of the twelfth verse is subject and which predicate, explain that the verb of the thirteenth does not properly mean winking since it is used of the lips as well as the eyes but unites the senses of pinching with a sharp and a blunt instrument, prefer the unfettering of the winds by Aeolus to the apple of discord as the figure of the fourteenth, take the breaking of the fifteenth as that of a brittle potter’s vessel, and draw the point of the climax, that no vice is a greater abomination than the striving to set at variance men who love one another; Ellicott sees in the thirteenth verse a malicious tattler filling out his tale with signs, and sets out the numerical form, its name and the places where it occurs.

debates: What are the signs of the thirteenth verse? Clarke takes them for the signals of debauchees and quotes a Latin elegy in which a lover instructs his mistress how to signal at a banquet, by the foot, the eyebrows and words traced in spilt wine. Ellicott sees a malicious tattler instead, filling out a lying tale with winks so that more is suggested than said. Gill keeps the middle ground, a sneering man giving a friend the wink at another’s weakness, and Keil and Delitzsch avoid the question by working on the verb, which they say does not properly mean winking at all.
outliers: Clarke quotes a Latin elegy at length and then declines to give the rest, remarking that though it has been translated it cannot be introduced here.

Ellicott sets out the numerical form of the sixteenth verse, names it after later writers, lists the places where it occurs, and observes that in all of them the first number is afterwards increased by one, a peculiarity three other instances lack.
Keil and Delitzsch prefer one classical figure to another for the sowing of discord, the unfettering of the winds rather than the casting in of the apple.
Ellicott judges the mischief-maker the worst of the seven things named, being described in like terms in a psalm and placed last in the climax here.
themes: a name better left untranslated
a lover’s signals or a tattler’s
a quotation cut short by decency
six things hated and a seventh worse
pride first because first committed

20.pericope_label: My son, keep thy father’s commandment: for the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light: to keep thee from the evil woman

schools.summary: Henry divides the word into a light to which the understanding must subscribe by its arguments and a law to which the will must submit by its authority, holding that no light ever shone from the schools of the philosophers like it and no law so well framed or so binding ever issued from the throne of a prince.

Gill is careful that the words are the writer’s own and not the father’s of an earlier chapter, addressed to everyone who came to him for instruction and to everyone standing in that relation to a religious father, keeps the leading of the twenty-second verse to the law directing what way to shun and which to walk in, and draws the practical link at the end, that the law directs to duties which require diligence and so prevent idleness, that inlet to all sin.

Clarke refers the commandment and the binding to earlier chapters and to the command about writing the words on the hand and doorpost, personifies the law as a nurse, teacher and guardian by night and day so that a man commends himself to his Maker on lying down and wakes to the promises of God, and turns personal at the twenty-fourth verse, remarking that the writer had suffered sorely from that quarter and defining the strange woman as one not a man’s own and possibly a foreigner; Wesley puts the whole first verse in eight words.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the twentieth verse as a return to the theme of an earlier section after three shorter ones, note the reference of the suffix and the figure of the phylactery, hold that the personified doctrine of the twenty-second verse gives promises and not wishes in the order of an older formula, distinguish the light as general from the lamp kindled at it, and reject a rendering of the twenty-fourth verse adopted by two scholars and two Greek versions; Ellicott turns the lamp and light into counsel for a man in perplexity, who by following the part of his duty he knows prepares himself for more light.

debates: How are the lamp and the light related? Keil and Delitzsch make them general and particular, the instruction being the light that enlightens the man who submits to it and the commandment a lamp kindled at that light for the darkness of ignorance about conduct; they add that the word for instruction has here the general sense of teaching about the will of God rather than its specifically national one. Clarke keeps them parallel, the commandment illuminating the path and the law showing the nature and will of God. Henry divides them by faculty instead, the word being light to the understanding by its arguments and law to the will by its authority.
outliers: Ellicott turns the verse into counsel for a man who cannot see his way, that there is always some command he cannot doubt and some discipline he knows, and that by following what he knows he prepares himself for more light.
Clarke reads the repeated warnings against the strange woman biographically, remarking that the writer had suffered sorely from that quarter.
Henry sets the word above both philosophy and legislation, since no such light ever shone from the schools nor such a law issued from any throne.

Keil and Delitzsch reject a rendering of the twenty-fourth verse held by two scholars and two old Greek versions, on the ground that the noun in question is not an adjective and the anomaly assumed is unnecessary.
themes: a theme returned to after three digressions
teaching that leads, watches and talks
a lamp kindled at a light
light enough for the next step
a warning repeated from experience

25.pericope_label: Lust not after her beauty in thine heart: can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the eye that kindles lust from the thought that cherishes it, keeps the received reading of the piece of bread and applies it to the man reduced to begging a morsel, quotes a Greek sage on the fire, canvasses three explanations of the sevenfold restitution and prefers perfect restitution as often as the thief is found guilty, and offers three sources for the wound of the thirty-third verse, the husband, the magistrate, or diseases sent by God.

Clarke explains the eyelids from the eastern custom of painting them with a preparation of antimony so that the eyes take an indescribable lustre, reports the Greek reading that makes the hire of a harlot a single loaf and the sense that while the man hires for a loaf the woman takes his life, says the questions about fire were proverbial expressions plain to every capacity, notes that no law clears the hungry thief who must still make restitution or be sold, and supplies a Roman punishment for the adulterer so disgraceful that it commonly caused his death; Wesley makes the sevenfold restitution what the wronged man might exact or the thief give to avoid public shame.

Keil and Delitzsch set the warning beside the tenth commandment and the sentence of the Sermon on the Mount and cite a Talmudic saying that the imagination of a sinful act exhausts the body more than the act, quote a Greek sage that falling into fire and into a woman are the same, note that the verb for burning leaves a brand-mark and that the phrases of the twenty-ninth verse are euphemisms, dispute the usual explanation of the thirtieth verse as resting on a sense devised for the passage alone, and hold that one stolen from may be appeased but not an injured husband; Ellicott makes the thief more worthy of pity than disdain and able to make retribution as the adulterer is not, and reads the sevenfold restitution as permission rather than requirement.

debates: What does the sevenfold restitution mean? Gill canvasses a Jewish authority who reaches the number by adding the double and the fivefold that the law prescribes, others who suppose a foreign law or a penalty increased in the writer’s own time, and his own preference, that it means perfect restitution as often as the thief is found guilty. Ellicott reads it as permission rather than requirement, since the law required less and the thief may do even more, and takes the number for full restitution. Wesley makes it neither the law’s requirement nor a permission but what the wronged man might exact or the thief would give to avoid public shame.
outliers: Clarke explains the catching eyelids from cosmetics, the eastern practice of polishing the eyes with antimony so that, as one observer wrote, they appear to be swimming in bliss.
Gill and Keil and Delitzsch independently quote the same Greek philosopher on the twenty-seventh verse, that to fall into fire and into a woman come to the same thing.
Clarke reports a Greek reading in which the hire of a harlot is a single loaf, so many being such women in the land that they hired themselves for a bare subsistence.
Keil and Delitzsch state the ground of the whole comparison, that one who has been stolen from may be appeased but not an injured husband.
themes: eyes polished with antimony
a life taken for a loaf
fire and a woman in one saying
a thief pitied and an adulterer not
restitution required, permitted, or extorted
